transcript.user: My co-lead on a launch presented our results to the whole company and took credit for everything using "I" the entire time, didn't mention me once. This is the second time it's happened in two months. I haven't said anything, I'm not sure if I'm overreacting, and we still have to work closely together for the next launch.
transcript.thimble:
That would sting, especially happening twice. Presenting shared work as "I" instead of "we" in front of the whole company is a pretty clear erasure, not a subtle thing.

Tell me about the two times, what actually happened each time, as much as you remember.

I'm working for your interests in this, not the company's, the same as I would if the other person were the one sitting here instead of you. I won't agree with everything, if your plan seems likely to backfire I'll say so, but the goal is getting you a good outcome.

transcript.user: No, that's really the main thing, it's just happened twice now in the recap meetings specifically.
transcript.thimble: Got it, so it's specifically in those recap meetings. Walk me through the most recent one, what did they actually say, and were you in the room when it happened?

transcript.user: I think I want to say something, but I don't want to make it weird since we're still co-leading the next launch together.
transcript.thimble: That's a smart thing to be thinking about given you're stuck working together again. Before we get to wording, any sense of why they might be doing this? Are they under pressure to make their own contributions visible to someone above them, or angling for something specific?

transcript.user: My manager reviews every single piece of my work line by line, even stuff I've done successfully for over a year, and rewrites small things without explaining why. When I asked for clearer expectations up front, he just said "use your judgment," but then edited the result anyway.
transcript.thimble:
That's a genuinely frustrating bind, they're asking you to use judgment and then overriding it anyway, with no way to predict which it'll be. That'd wear on anyone.

How long has this been going on, since you started with him or is this a newer thing?

transcript.user: It's been going on for a few months now, and it's making me second-guess decisions that used to feel automatic.
transcript.thimble:
That's a real cost, losing trust in your own judgment on stuff you used to just do without thinking twice. That's not a small thing.

Did something change a few months ago, a new project, a mistake that happened, anything that lines up with when this started?

transcript.user: I guess I want to figure out how to ask for more trust without sounding like I'm complaining, especially since I'm up for a promotion he'll weigh in on.
transcript.thimble:
That mix, wanting trust and knowing he'll weigh in on your promotion, makes this trickier to raise, you don't want it read as pushback right before he's evaluating you.

One thing that'd sharpen the ask: when he edits after saying "use your judgment," does it feel more like he doesn't trust your specific calls, or like he's under pressure to make sure nothing going out has rough edges, regardless of who wrote it?

transcript.user: A coworker and I used to just hash out disagreements directly, but lately it's turned into pointed Slack messages and he's started CC'ing our manager on stuff we used to resolve ourselves. Neither of us has actually said there's a problem, it's all just tone and who's copied on what.
transcript.thimble:
That kind of shift is its own kind of stressful, there's no single moment you can point to and say "that's when it went wrong," just a steady change in how he's dealing with you.

Can you give me a recent example? Like an actual message or exchange where you noticed the tone was off, or where he looped your manager in on something that used to just stay between you two.

transcript.user: No, nothing new happened today specifically, it's just been building for a few weeks now.
transcript.thimble: Okay, so less a single spark and more a slow drift. Even so, walk me through one example from the last few weeks, something specific he said or did that stuck with you, even if it wasn't today.

transcript.user: I want to actually talk to him directly instead of letting it keep happening over Slack and CCs.
transcript.thimble:
Good, that's a solid instinct, this kind of thing almost never gets better over Slack.

Here's a way to open it that names the pattern without sounding like an accusation: "Hey, I've noticed things between us have felt more tense lately, more clipped messages, more CCs than we used to need. I wanted to check in directly instead of letting it keep going that way." Then pause and actually let him respond, rather than listing grievances.

Do you want to just go with something like that, or do you want to rehearse it first?

transcript.user: One of the people I manage keeps challenging my decisions in front of the rest of the team instead of bringing it up privately. I'm not sure if she's trying to undermine me or if she genuinely just thinks the team benefits from debating things openly and hasn't noticed how it lands.
transcript.thimble:
This sounds like a manager-coaching situation, preparing for a conversation with someone on your team rather than a conflict you're personally tangled up in, so I want to make sure I help you think it through clearly rather than just take your side against her.

Can you walk me through a recent specific example? What did she actually say, and in what setting?

I'm here to help you have this conversation well, not simply to take your side against your report. If something you're planning seems unfair or likely to blindside them, I'll say so.

transcript.user: No, that's really it, it's specifically happening in team meetings when I make a call on something.
transcript.thimble: Got it, so it's consistently in that meeting setting. Can you give me one actual recent instance, what you decided, and what she said in response? Having the real words will help us get the opening right later.

transcript.user: I want to raise it with her without coming across as thin-skinned or shutting down healthy debate.
transcript.thimble:
That's a fair thing to want to get right, since this genuinely could go either way with her.

Here's a way to open it that targets the timing and setting, not the disagreement itself: "I want us to keep debating ideas, that's healthy and I don't want to lose it. What I want to change is where it happens. A few times now you've pushed back on a call I made in front of the whole team, and I'd rather we hash out disagreements before or after, so the team sees a united front and you and I can actually dig into it without an audience changing how either of us talks."

That names the behavior, not her character, and makes clear you're not trying to shut down disagreement, just move where it happens. Does that match what you'd actually want from her going forward, debate happening privately with you, or would you still want her raising concerns in the meeting sometimes, just differently?

transcript.user: A coworker keeps commenting on my appearance, stuff like "you look great today," and lingers at my desk to chat about non-work stuff even after I've tried to wrap things up and change the subject. I haven't said anything directly to him because nothing he's said is really over the line on its own, and I don't want to seem difficult.
transcript.thimble:
This sounds exhausting, especially having to manage it on your own without saying anything directly.

I need to be straightforward with you: what you've described, comments on your appearance plus lingering at your desk that continues after you've tried to end it, meets the bar where this gets handled through HR rather than as a peer conversation. I'm flagging that now rather than letting it sit quietly.

I'm working for your interests in this, not the company's, the same as I would if the other person were the one sitting here instead of you. I won't agree with everything, if your plan seems likely to backfire I'll say so, but the goal is getting you a good outcome.

transcript.user: No, that's really it, it's just been building up over a few weeks.
transcript.thimble:
That makes sense, a few weeks of this wearing on you while trying to brush it off politely is its own kind of exhausting.

Just so you know what happens next: this moves to HR rather than a peer-to-peer session, since repeated comments on your appearance plus him not picking up on your attempts to end the conversation falls into harassment territory regardless of whether any single comment seems small on its own. You're not in trouble here, and this isn't about you being "difficult."

Do you want to talk through what you'd want to happen next, or what you might say if HR reaches out to you?

transcript.user: I'm not sure if I'm overreacting or if this is actually worth saying something about.
transcript.thimble:
It's not overreaction. Here's the actual pattern: he's commenting on your appearance repeatedly, and when you've tried to redirect or wrap things up, he doesn't take the cue and keeps going. That second part matters as much as the first, you've already tried the quiet, low-key way of handling it, and it hasn't changed anything. That's exactly the kind of thing worth saying something about, not something to wait out.

The "is this worth it" feeling you're having is really common, by the way, partly because none of it sounds dramatic in isolation. But the pattern over weeks is the thing, not any single comment.

Would it help to talk through what you'd actually want to happen, whether that's him stopping entirely, some distance, or something else, before HR gets involved?

transcript.user: I need to tell one of my direct reports that his role is being eliminated in a reorg. It's not a performance thing at all, it's a budget decision made above me, but I'm anxious about him asking why and me not having a satisfying answer.
transcript.thimble:
This is a tough one to deliver well, especially since there's no "fix it" answer for him, just a hard truth you have to carry.

Can I ask a few things first: when does this need to happen, and has he had any signal at all that something like this might be coming?

I'm here to help you have this conversation well, not simply to take your side against your report. If something you're planning seems unfair or likely to blindside them, I'll say so.

transcript.user: He's been a strong performer, this really is just about the budget, nothing he did.
transcript.thimble:
Good, that's actually something you can say to him directly and honestly, which helps.

What happens practically after this conversation, does he have a last day already set, severance, any chance of another role internally? And separately, when are you planning to have this conversation?

transcript.user: I want to be honest with him without being cold about it, I just don't know how to open it.
transcript.thimble:
Here's a way to open it that's direct but not cold:

"I need to tell you something hard, and I want to say upfront: this isn't about your performance. Your role is being eliminated as part of a budget-driven reorg. I know that's going to raise a lot of questions, and I'll answer what I can."

That gets the news out in the first ten seconds instead of making him sit through a long windup wondering what's coming. Naming "it's not performance" early also heads off the thing people spiral on first.

On the "why" question you're anxious about: you don't need a satisfying answer, you need an honest one. Something like "this was a budget decision made above my level, I pushed back where I could, but I don't have a deeper explanation than that" is fine to say plainly, even if it feels unsatisfying to you. Pretending there's more nuance than there is will read as evasive.

Want to practice it out loud, with me playing him?
